summary: Clarifies and extends the Bootstrap Protocol, strengthening the descriptions of BOOTP relay agents, originally called forwarding agents, and of client behavior.

eli5.summary: This memo makes the rules for how a startup helper and a message passer should act much clearer.

questions: what is a bootp relay agent
what is the bootp broadcast flag
what is the bootp giaddr field
subtitle: Tightens up the rules for BOOTP clients, servers and relay agents, and gives the old unused field a job as the BROADCAST flag.

tldr.problem: The original BOOTP specification left open how relay agents should behave, how several fields should be used, and how to cope with IEEE 802.5 Token Ring networks.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines the 'flags' field with a BROADCAST bit, pins down client, server and relay agent behavior field by field, and gives a delivery table for BOOTREPLY messages.
tldr.outcome: It updates RFC 951 and obsoletes RFC 1532, which was reissued as this RFC after editorial errors. The same rules also apply to extensions such as DHCP.

today: RFC 1542 is a Draft Standard that obsoletes RFC 1532 and updates RFC 951. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why BOOTP Needed Clarifying
sections.content:
The Bootstrap Protocol (BOOTP) is a UDP/IP-based protocol that lets a booting host configure itself without user supervision. It can tell a host its IP address, the address of a boot server and the name of a file to load. Other settings, such as the subnet mask and default routers, can be passed using the vendor information extensions in RFC 1497.

The original specification, RFC 951, left several things open. The behavior of BOOTP relay agents (formerly called forwarding agents) was not clearly specified, some parts conflicted, and others were easy to misread. This memo clarifies them and also proposes a solution for IEEE 802.5 Token Ring networks.

The memo is a reissue of RFC 1532, because some errors were introduced into that RFC during editing. Unless stated otherwise, its requirements also apply to extensions of BOOTP such as DHCP (RFC 1541).
sections.eli5: BOOTP is how a computer asks the network who it is when it wakes up. The first rulebook had gaps, so this one fills them in.

sections.title: The Flags Field and General Message Rules
sections.content:
The BOOTP message has a two-octet field between 'secs' and 'ciaddr' that the original specification called merely unused. This memo names it the flags field. Its most significant bit is the BROADCAST (B) flag. The remaining bits are reserved: clients MUST set them to zero, and servers and relay agents ignore them.

All BOOTP entities SHOULD run consistency checks. The IP and UDP lengths must be large enough for the minimal BOOTP header of 300 octets, and larger messages MUST still be accepted because future extensions may grow the message. The 'op' field must be 1 (BOOTREQUEST) or 2 (BOOTREPLY). Messages that fail are silently discarded, meaning no ICMP error is sent, though implementations SHOULD log the event and count it.

The hardware address in 'chaddr' SHOULD use the same bit ordering as ARP on the client's link. A relay agent MUST NOT reverse that ordering, even when relaying between networks with different orderings. For example, a client on IEEE 802.5 Token Ring uses the opposite bit ordering from a client on DIX Ethernet.

The reason 'chaddr' exists is to let servers and relay agents talk directly to clients without broadcasts, often by creating an ARP cache entry from it.
sections.eli5: There was an empty box on the form. Now its first square means 'please shout my answer to everyone', and the checks say to throw away forms that look wrong.

sections.title: How Clients Should Behave
sections.content:
Servers and relay agents normally unicast a reply to the client's 'yiaddr' address and 'chaddr' hardware address. Some old clients cannot receive unicast datagrams before they know their own address. Such a client SHOULD set the BROADCAST flag to 1 as a hint to broadcast the reply. A client that can receive unicast SHOULD leave it clear. The memo calls this a workaround and discourages its use.

The 'secs' field SHOULD hold the seconds elapsed since the client sent its first BOOTREQUEST, so the first request has zero. Clients SHOULD NOT use a constant value. The 'ciaddr' field SHOULD be 0.0.0.0 if the client does not know its address. The memo discusses several interpretations and calls the one where the client always puts 0.0.0.0 there the safest. If a client does fill it in, it MUST accept unicasts to that address and answer ARP for it.

The 'giaddr' field is, in the memo's words, rather poorly named. A client MUST set it to zero in requests, and MUST NOT treat the 'giaddr' of a reply as the address of a router. To reach a non-local server it can use the Gateway subfield of the vendor extensions or ICMP router discovery (RFC 1256).

Clients are also RECOMMENDED to start the 'vend' field with a four-octet magic cookie. Without a vendor-specific one they SHOULD use the dotted decimal value 99.130.83.99, followed by the End tag (255) if there is nothing to say.
sections.eli5: A kid who cannot hear a whisper can ask to be called out loud. The kid should also say how long they have been waiting and leave the 'send me to the boss' box empty.

sections.title: BOOTP Relay Agents
sections.content:
When clients and servers sit on different networks, a relay agent transfers messages between them. It is not a normal router forwarding. It receives a BOOTP message as a final destination and generates a new one, and it MUST NOT pass the message straight through like a regular packet. The function is often located in a router but can be in a host on the client subnet.

A relay agent considers UDP messages sent to port BOOTPS (67). It MUST accept requests whose IP source is 0.0.0.0, despite normal filtering of illegal source addresses, and MUST silently discard anything sent to BOOTPC (68). Relaying MUST be disabled by default, and the relay destination MUST be configurable.

For a BOOTREQUEST, the relay agent silently discards requests whose 'hops' field exceeds 16 (the configurable default threshold SHOULD be 4). If 'giaddr' is zero, it MUST fill it with the address of the receiving interface. A non-zero 'giaddr' MUST NOT be changed, and it must never be a broadcast address. It increments 'hops' and preserves all other fields. All requests from one client MUST go to the same destination or set of destinations, because DHCP depends on multiple exchanges. Hashing the client's link-layer address is one way to balance load.

For a BOOTREPLY, the servers send replies directly to the address in 'giaddr', so the relay agent assumes every reply is for a client on a directly connected network. If 'giaddr' matches none of its interfaces, the reply is silently discarded. Otherwise it delivers by broadcast to 255.255.255.255 when the BROADCAST flag is 1, or by unicast to 'yiaddr' and 'chaddr' when it is 0. The UDP destination port MUST be BOOTPC (68), and the agent MUST NOT modify any BOOTP field.
sections.eli5: A relay agent is a mail clerk between two towns. It copies the letter, writes its own town on it, and later brings the answer back to the right door.

sections.title: How Servers Deliver Replies
sections.content:
A BOOTP server considers UDP messages for port BOOTPS (67), MUST accept requests from source 0.0.0.0, and MUST silently discard messages for port BOOTPC (68). It MAY use 'secs' when deciding whether to reply. It SHOULD NOT trust 'ciaddr' alone to identify a client, and SHOULD copy 'ciaddr' unchanged into the reply.

To deliver a reply, the server checks fields in order. If 'ciaddr' is non-zero, it SHOULD unicast to that address with port BOOTPC (68), though it MAY ignore 'ciaddr'. Otherwise, if 'giaddr' is non-zero, it SHOULD unicast to the relay agent with port BOOTPS (67) and preserve the BROADCAST flag. If both are zero, the client is on the server's own network, so the server broadcasts if the flag is set, or unicasts to 'yiaddr' and 'chaddr' if not.
sections.eli5: The server looks at the note to decide how to answer. If it has a return address it uses it. If a helper passed the note, the answer goes to the helper. Otherwise it calls out or hands the answer over directly.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The memo says BOOTP in its current form is quite insecure. It is built directly on UDP and IP, and its use for remote and diskless hosts makes configuring passwords or keys inconvenient, so reasonable authentication between servers and clients is hard.

Unauthorized BOOTP servers are easy to set up. They can send false information such as incorrect or duplicate IP addresses, spoof routers or spoof name servers. Unauthorized relay agents pose similar problems. Malicious clients can masquerade as legitimate ones to retrieve their information, or claim all dynamically allocated resources.
sections.eli5: Anyone can pretend to be the helper and give a new computer wrong directions. The protocol has no good way to check who is telling the truth.

viz.caption: BOOTP MESSAGE FORMAT (FIELD SIZES IN OCTETS, RFC 1542)

fields.name: secs
fields.desc: Seconds since the client sent its first BOOTREQUEST.

fields.name: flags
fields.desc: Top bit is the BROADCAST flag; the rest must be zero.

fields.name: ciaddr
fields.desc: Client IP address, if the client knows it.

fields.name: yiaddr
fields.desc: IP address assigned to the client by the server.

fields.name: giaddr
fields.desc: Set by the relay agent to the receiving interface address.

items.label: UDP 68 to ciaddr
items.desc: Unicast to the client address; link layer determined normally.

items.label: UDP 67 to giaddr
items.desc: Unicast to the relay agent when ciaddr is 0.0.0.0.

items.label: UDP 68 to yiaddr
items.desc: Unicast to yiaddr, link layer address from chaddr.

items.label: UDP 68 to 255.255.255.255
items.desc: Broadcast at IP and link layer.
